author: Ben Ellsworth
text:
An ML engineer and an AI engineer are not the same hire.

You are about to pay for the wrong one.

An ML engineer trains and evaluates models. They live in experiments and metrics. Their instinct is to make the model better.

An AI engineer takes a model that already works and makes it survive contact with real users. Their instinct is to ship it and contain the damage when it is wrong.

Most startups do not need a new model. They need the second person.

But the post says ML engineer, because that is the title everyone knows, so that is who applies.

Then the model person lands, asks for a training budget and a bigger GPU, and the actual product work sits.

Six months later the founder tells me hiring is broken.

Hiring is not broken. You wrote the wrong word at the top of the post and got exactly who it asked for.

Decide which instinct your roadmap needs before you name the role.

One wants to improve the model. The other wants to make your product work. Those are rarely the same person.

author: Narendran Poyyamozhi
text:
Data science isn't dying.
Your version of it is.


Here is what nobody wants to say out loud: the job you were hired for in 2022 doesn't exist anymore. And AI didn't kill it. It just made half of it disposable.

Look at the postings data. Entry-level data analyst and junior data scientist postings are down sharply at mid-to-large tech companies. But the roles that disappeared weren't the ones building production ML systems. 

They were the ones doing dashboards, ad hoc SQL, cleaning data for someone else. Those tasks didn't vanish. One person with AI now does them in an afternoon.

Meanwhile the postings that are exploding look nothing like your current title.

AI engineering job postings are up 800% this year. Roles in data engineering and AI scalability are projected to grow 414%. Hiring managers for these roles want repos, deployed agents, and eval suites, not credentials. And the pay reflects it: a 56% wage premium for roles that explicitly require AI skills over ones that don't.

So the real question isn't "is data science dead."
It is: which of the four jobs it split into are you becoming?

Ask yourself two things.
Are you closer to the model, or closer to the business?
Are you building things, or governing them?

Those two questions put you in one of four lanes:
→ Model-facing, building: Context/AI Engineer
→ Model-facing, governing: AI Evals/Reliability Engineer
→ Business-facing, building: Analytics Translator
→ Business-facing, governing: AI Product Manager

Notice something. Not one of these four is "the person who makes the dashboard." That job is gone, and it isn't coming back.

Pick a lane before the market picks one for you.

Which quadrant are you actually in right now, not the one on your title, the one you're doing every day?

author: Sayam Muzafar
text:
Everyone wants to become an ML Engineer.

But in 2026...

Many companies are hiring AI Engineers instead.

Why?

Because most businesses don't need to build foundation models.

They need people who can ship AI products.

That's a completely different skill set.

Here's the difference 👇

🧠 ML Engineers build the intelligence

They work on:

✅ Training models from scratch
✅ Fine-tuning neural networks
✅ PyTorch, TensorFlow, Scikit-learn
✅ Feature engineering & data pipelines
✅ Experiment tracking & hyperparameter tuning
✅ Model deployment & monitoring

This is deep, research-heavy engineering.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

⚡AI Engineers build the product

They work on:

✅ GPT-5, Claude, Gemini, Llama APIs
✅ RAG pipelines & Vector Databases
✅ AI Agents (LangGraph, CrewAI, LangChain)
✅ FastAPI, Vercel & AWS Lambda
✅ OpenAI, Anthropic, Vertex AI & Bedrock APIs
✅ Evaluation, observability & production workflows

This is product-first engineering.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

The market shift

Today, most companies aren't asking:

"Can you train a billion-parameter model?"

They're asking:

→ Can you build an AI assistant?
→ Can you automate our workflows?
→ Can you deploy an internal chatbot?
→ Can you integrate AI into our product?

That's why AI Engineering has become one of the fastest-growing software roles.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

Reality check

ML Engineers create the models.

AI Engineers create products people actually use.

Both careers are valuable.

They simply solve different problems.

If you're starting today and want to build real-world AI applications quickly, AI Engineering is one of the fastest paths into modern AI development.

If you enjoy mathematics, optimization, and model research, ML Engineering remains an excellent career path.

The strongest engineers understand both.

🧠 ML Engineer

⚡ AI Engineer

author: Pooja Jain
text:
"Data Engineer" is not one job. 
It is 6 distinct specializations.

Most companies advertise for one and end up hiring for another. Most engineers pick a lane and never realize how different the others are.

Here are the 6 types of data engineers, each with a different focus, tool stack, and career ceiling:

𝐄𝐓𝐋 / 𝐄𝐋𝐓 𝐄𝐧𝐠𝐢𝐧𝐞𝐞𝐫 
Focus: ingest, transform, load data across systems 
→ Tools: Fivetran, Airbyte, dbt, Airflow, Dagster 
↳ The backbone role that keeps analytics and BI running

𝐏𝐥𝐚𝐭𝐟𝐨𝐫𝐦 / 𝐃𝐚𝐭𝐚 𝐈𝐧𝐟𝐫𝐚 𝐄𝐧𝐠𝐢𝐧𝐞𝐞𝐫 
Focus: build the data platform other DEs use 
→ Tools: Kubernetes, Terraform, Kafka, Spark, custom internal tooling 
↳ Enables the whole data org, highest ceiling for scale and compensation

𝐀𝐧𝐚𝐥𝐲𝐭𝐢𝐜𝐬 / 𝐁𝐈 𝐃𝐚𝐭𝐚 𝐄𝐧𝐠𝐢𝐧𝐞𝐞𝐫 
Focus: build the tables, models, and metrics analysts consume 
→ Tools: dbt, Snowflake, Databricks, Looker, semantic layer 
↳ Closest to the business, translates raw data into decision-ready models

𝐌𝐋 𝐃𝐚𝐭𝐚 𝐄𝐧𝐠𝐢𝐧𝐞𝐞𝐫 
Focus: build feature stores, training pipelines, vector infra for ML and AI 
→ Tools: Feast, Tecton, MLflow, Pinecone, Databricks Feature Store 
↳ Fastest-growing lane in 2026, bridges DE and ML seamlessly

𝐃𝐚𝐭𝐚𝐎𝐩𝐬 / 𝐃𝐚𝐭𝐚 𝐑𝐞𝐥𝐢𝐚𝐛𝐢𝐥𝐢𝐭𝐲 𝐄𝐧𝐠𝐢𝐧𝐞𝐞𝐫 
Focus: SLAs, monitoring, incident response, data quality at scale 
→ Tools: Monte Carlo, Elementary, Datadog, PagerDuty, custom observability 
↳ SRE for data · on-call for the freshness dashboard

𝐂𝐥𝐨𝐮𝐝 𝐃𝐚𝐭𝐚 𝐄𝐧𝐠𝐢𝐧𝐞𝐞𝐫 
 Focus: cloud-native architecture across AWS, Azure, or GCP
→ Tools: Redshift, BigQuery, Snowflake, Glue, Dataflow, Synapse 
↳ Deep in one cloud, often owns cost optimization and governance

Across all 6 roles, the shared foundation stays the same:

SQL
Python or Scala 
Data modeling 
Git and CI/CD 
Data quality awareness

The best data engineers are not just tool users.

They are systems thinkers. 
They understand the trade-offs behind every tool choice. 
They know why a system was built and where it will fail at scale. 

The gap between "I know the tools" and "I know why the tools exist" is where senior data engineers separate from the crowd.

Pick your lane. 
Go deep. 
But never stop learning the other 5.

Which type of data engineer are you today? 👇

author: Alex Tiley
text:
Does your strategy require a unicorn?        Switching gears from risk tolerance and personal use to corporate AI strategy — what direction are you heading in? Open-weight or closed-weight? 

Open-weight AI models aren't necessarily less secure than closed-weight ones, they're just differently secure, and the difference comes down to something that can get overlooked: people 

The surprise? the headcount is the same.
An organisation with proper AI governance is likely to already have 4-5 people covering security, safety, infrastructure, monitoring, and compliance (approach agnostic). The roles don't change, but the complexity, effort and work upfront does.
The real difference: skill depth.
Closed-weight security is application-layer work. API security, prompt engineering, vendor risk. A mid-career engineer (2-5 years) can cover it. Open-weight demands model-layer expertise — adversarial ML, Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF), alignment training — in theory the disciplines requiring 8+ years, where the techniques themselves have only existed for 3-5.

The unicorn problem:
The open-weight AI safety engineer needs RLHF expertise, architecture depth, fine-tuning ops, and the judgement to make safety trade-offs. Most people with this profile are inside frontier labs. The number available for enterprise hiring is in the double digits globally.

However, there are ways around it:
Decompose the unicorn — split it into a safety researcher + fine-tuning engineer. Neither alone is impossible to hire.
Buy the safety layer — use pre-aligned open models (Llama, Mistral) and invest in evaluation over alignment. Trade-off: you're trusting someone else's safety work again.
Grow your own — hire a strong ML engineer and invest 12-18 months in up-skilling. Slowest path, but builds durable capability.

The bottom line:
The gap between open and closed isn't filled with technology — it's filled with talent. If your evaluation compares features, pricing, and benchmarks without asking "do we have the people to secure this?" — you're creating exposure.
Are you finding the talent to make open-weight work, or is the skills gap pushing you toward closed providers?

What a BTech Data Science Graduate Can Actually Do in 2026

"Data Scientist" has become the label everyone chases. But here's what most students miss: the field has quietly split into several distinct roles — and "Data Scientist" is just one of them.

That shift matters, because it changes what you should actually prepare for.
A few years ago, one person cleaned data, built models, and presented insights. Today those tasks have specialised. NASSCOM and LinkedIn's "Jobs on the Rise" reports have repeatedly flagged data and AI roles among the fastest-growing in India — but the demand is spreading across roles, not just one title.

Here's what a BTech CSE (Data Science) graduate can realistically move into:
*Data Analyst — turning raw numbers into business decisions using SQL, Excel, and Power BI
*Machine Learning Engineer — deploying models into real products (think recommendation systems)
*Data Engineer — building the pipelines that make data usable (increasingly in demand)
*Business Intelligence Analyst — dashboards and reporting that drive strategy
AI / ML Specialist — working on NLP, computer vision, and generative AI

Notice the range. A student who assumes "Data Science = one job" often misses the role that actually fits them best.

Why this matters: the graduates getting hired aren't the ones who only know theory. They're the ones who've built real projects — a working model, a dashboard, a cleaned dataset analysed end to end. Tools like Python, SQL, and cloud platforms are now baseline expectations, not bonuses.

This is where the learning environment counts. At Amity University Patna, the BTech CSE (Data Science) program (https://lnkd.in/gTqaqeEQ) leans on an industry-oriented curriculum, hands-on labs, and project and research exposure — aiming to help students build practical, job-ready skills rather than just clear exams.

So here's my question to students, parents, and hiring professionals: In 2026, what matters more when hiring a data science graduate — the degree and marks, or the projects and tools they can actually demonstrate? I'd genuinely like your view.

Today, I officially received my 𝗠𝗮𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗿 𝗼𝗳 𝗦𝗰𝗶𝗲𝗻𝗰𝗲 (𝘄𝗶𝘁𝗵 𝗠𝗲𝗿𝗶𝘁) in 𝗔𝗿𝘁𝗶𝗳𝗶𝗰𝗶𝗮𝗹 𝗜𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗹𝗹𝗶𝗴𝗲𝗻𝗰𝗲 & 𝗠𝗮𝗰𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗲 𝗟𝗲𝗮𝗿𝗻𝗶𝗻𝗴 degree from Liverpool John Moores University. This milestone means far more than adding another qualification—it represents resilience, curiosity, and growth.

𝗧𝗟;𝗗𝗥 👀
✔️ MSc (with Merit) in AI & ML from LJMU
✔️ Hands-on experience building an end-to-end VideoRAG system
✔️ Practical exposure to LLMs, RAG, Multimodal AI, Vector Databases & AI Evaluation
✔️ Stronger foundation for AI Engineering, Enterprise AI & AI Architecture roles

The most defining part of this journey was my dissertation:
"Enriching Visual Question Answering using VideoRAG in the Medical Domain using the MedVidQA Dataset."

It was one of the most ambitious and technically challenging topics I could have chosen within the limited timeline.

The goal was to build an end-to-end AI system capable of understanding complex medical videos, retrieving the most relevant context, generating accurate answers using LLMs, and pinpointing the exact video timestamps.

The journey wasn't easy. From GPU and infrastructure limitations to long experimentation cycles, integrating multiple AI components, and balancing research alongside a full-time job, there were moments when I genuinely questioned whether I'd make it to the finish line.

But every challenge became a lesson.

I learnt that building impactful AI isn't about finding the perfect model—it's about designing reliable systems, making informed trade-offs, embracing failure, and continuously iterating.

This experience gave me practical exposure to VideoRAG, RAG, Multimodal AI, Visual Question Answering, LLMs, Prompt Engineering, Embedding Models, Vector Databases, Semantic Retrieval, and GenAI evaluation frameworks—while fundamentally changing the way I approach problem-solving.

More importantly, it has made me a stronger engineer today and strengthened my foundation for the next phase of my career in AI Engineering, Enterprise AI, and AI Architecture.

A heartfelt thank you to my professors, mentors, peers and friends at upGrad and Liverpool John Moores University, to my family and to everyone who supported me throughout this journey.

Here's to staying curious, taking on daunting challenges, and never stopping learning. Onwards and Upwards. 🚀

When hiring AI talent don't just look for people who can build models, look for people who can solve business problems.
A few recommendations for companies hiring AI professionals:

• Define the business outcome before writing the job description.
• Hire for curiosity and adaptability as much as technical expertise, AI changes too quickly to hire only for today's tools.
• Don't expect one person to be a Data Scientist, ML Engineer, AI Architect, Prompt Engineer, Product Manager and Change Lead.
• Assess real-world problem solving rather than relying on technical interviews alone.
• Prioritise communication skills. The best AI professionals can explain complex concepts to non-technical stakeholders.
• Make sure your data, governance and leadership are ready. AI projects often fail because of organisational issues, not technical ones.
• Be realistic on experience. There are very few people with 10+ years of AI experience because modern generative AI is still new.
• Move quickly. The strongest AI candidates rarely stay on the market for long.

The companies getting the best AI talent aren't necessarily paying the most, they're offering interesting problems, supportive leadership, clear strategy and the opportunity to make a genuine impact.
